paper.title: Scaling Sim-to-Real VLA Reinforcement Learning with Generative 3D Worlds

read: full text: Sections 1-5 and Appendices A (training details, domain randomisation, reward), B (effect of K), C (generation metrics, QA), D (model candidates), E-J (scene lists, real-world rollouts)

claims.claim: A pretrained vision-language-action manipulation policy can be improved by reinforcement learning carried out entirely in simulation, in tabletop scenes produced automatically by a 3D world generator from text task descriptions rather than designed by hand, and the improvement survives transfer to a physical robot. Supported only if, starting from the imitation-trained policy and using only a sparse success reward, the fine-tuned policy at least doubles the imitation policy's overall real-world pick-and-place success rate across at least ten real scenes that include objects absent from the simulated training scenes, and also raises success in simulation on the generated scenes it was trained on.
claims.decision_rule: Real-world overall SR at least 2x the imitation policy over >=10 real scenes with unseen objects; sim SR on generated scenes also rises.

claims.claim: When a pretrained manipulation policy is fine-tuned by reinforcement learning in simulation, training on more distinct generated scenes, meaning different backgrounds and object assets rather than just randomised poses, lighting and cameras, makes it generalise better zero-shot to scenes it never trained in, even at a fixed total compute budget. Supported only if success on held-out generated scenes rises at every step from 1 to 3 to 10 to 25 training scenes, and if on evaluation scenes built from other 3D asset sources never used in training, policies trained on 50 or more generated scenes beat single-scene training by at least 15 percentage points on each such source; and if a policy trained on a handful of hand-designed scenes generalises worse to those external scenes than one trained on the same number of generated scenes.
claims.decision_rule: Monotone rise in held-out generated-scene SR for N=1,3,10,25; >=15 pt gain over N=1 on each external asset source at N>=50; hand-designed-scene training generalises worse than equal-N generated.

experiments.text: Build the training scenes automatically and check their quality. Setup: a language-driven scene designer (GPT-4o) turns each pick-and-place instruction into a scene graph of background, context objects, distractors, target and robot with ON/IN relations; a text-to-3D world generator instantiates it as an interactive scene in a GPU-parallel simulator (ManiSkill3); an automated checker filters assets at three stages (image matches the object, mesh is intact, final 3D asset still matches the text) and resamples failures; oversized objects are scaled to fit a 74 mm gripper. Result: 100 scenes with 516 unique object assets (5.16 per scene); 1.37 generation attempts per accepted asset; 46.8 +/- 5.0 minutes per scene on one RTX 4090, or about 2 minutes with a reusable asset library; manual inspection finds 85% of scenes usable without intervention, the rest failing mainly on scale or placement.

Fix the starting policy and the reinforcement-learning recipe. Setup: start from a 3B flow-matching VLA (pi0) pretrained by imitation on BridgeV2, which is over 70% pick-and-place, run with 10 integration steps and 4-action chunks. Fine-tune with a PPO variant that injects learnable noise into a single integration step so action log-probabilities are defined, adding a value head, with a power-scaled importance ratio (0.2) for stability; LoRA on the vision-language backbone and full fine-tuning of the action expert; 192 parallel environments, batch 19,200, 25-step episodes at 5 Hz, 5 days on 8 RTX 6000 Ada GPUs. Reward is sparse: success only if the object touches the target and touches neither table nor robot. Randomise object position and yaw, robot height and joint positions, camera position and lighting, and use PD control with gravity compensation in both simulation and the real robot instead of system identification.

Measure the gain in simulation. Setup: evaluate the imitation policy and the policies fine-tuned on all 100 generated scenes, 100 episodes per scene, reporting success rate and time to finish over successful episodes. Result: success on the full generated set rises from 9.7% for the imitation policy to about 79% (78.9 +/- 0.9 over three seeds at N=100; the deployed checkpoint reaches 79.8%), and time to finish falls from about 10.0 s to 7.9-8.1 s.

Transfer to a physical robot. Setup: an Interbotix WidowX 250S with one external Logitech C922 webcam; 12 real tabletop scenes with distractors, several containing objects or attributes absent from simulated training (e.g. a screwdriver, a red knife among regular knives, teacup stacking); 10 trials per scene per policy, 240 trials in total, with object layouts re-randomised between trials. Measure partial success (target grasped and lifted), full success, failures from execution errors and failures from choosing the wrong object (not mutually exclusive), and time to finish. Result: partial success 45% to 88.3%, success 21.7% to 75%, execution-failure rate 66.7% to 18.3%, wrong-object rate 18.3% to 6.7%, time 11.5 s to 10.2 s; the unseen-screwdriver scene goes from 0% to 50% and teacup stacking from 20% to 50%.

Vary the number of distinct training scenes at fixed compute. Setup: draw three random 50-scene subsets of the 100 generated scenes; for each, the other 50 scenes are the held-out set. Train with the first N in {1, 3, 10, 25, 50} scenes of each subset (three runs per N, one per subset), plus three seeds on all 100, keeping batch and minibatch size fixed so each scene gets fewer samples as N grows. Evaluate 100 episodes per scene on the training scenes and on the held-out scenes. Result: training-scene success falls from 94.3% at N=1 to 80.5% at N=50 under the fixed budget, while held-out success rises 53.2%, 61.3%, 72.4%, 77.6%, 77.9% for N = 1, 3, 10, 25, 50, and the train-minus-held-out gap shrinks from 41.1 to 2.6 points. The gap is read alongside absolute held-out success, since it also shrinks when training-scene success falls.

Test generalisation to scenes from other asset sources. Setup: three evaluation sets never used in training: the three hand-designed SimplerEnv Bridge tabletop scenes (static backgrounds removed so randomisation applies), 18 scenes built from 25 Google Scanned Objects assets (18 semantically new), and 25 scenes built from 100 assets made by a different 3D generator (Hunyuan3D-2.1, 48 semantically new), all evaluated with domain randomisation on. Result: success rises with N on all three, from 36.1% at N=1 to 74.3% at N=100 on SimplerEnv, from 42.3% to 62.7% at N=25 on scanned objects, and from 42.7% to 63.3% at N=50 on the second generator's scenes; gains saturate around N = 25-50 and N=100 is slightly below the peak on scanned objects (60.7%).

Compare against fine-tuning on hand-designed scenes. Setup: run the same reinforcement learning on the three hand-designed SimplerEnv scenes only and evaluate on those scenes, on all 100 generated scenes and on the two external asset sets. Result: 96.7% success on its own three scenes but 36.0% on the generated scenes, 35.2% on scanned objects and 38.4% on the second generator's scenes, gaps of 58-61 points, against gaps of 27.4-41.3 points for policies trained on three generated scenes, which also reach 47.4-61.3% success on the same held-out sets.

dropped: Ablation over number of integration steps K in {1,2,4} (single run per setting, authors decline to interpret differences); training-strategy notes on freezing/LoRA (anecdotal, no numbers); foundation-model candidate notes.
notes: The fixed-compute confound (per-scene samples scale as 1/N, possibly causing the N=25-50 saturation) is conceded by the authors but not tested; left out of the experiment list.
